title: JudgeMix: Judge-Guided Mixed-Rollout Data Synthesis for LLM Agents
summary: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on expert trajectories is a standard paradigm for training LLM agents. However, it suffers from a well-known training-inference distribution mismatch, calling for target-aware data synthesis strategies that ground the training data in the target model's native state distribution. To bridge this gap, emerging approaches incorporate the expert either to guide mixed rollouts alongside the target model, or to provide dense step-wise supervision. Nonetheless, existing methods apply expert assistance blind to the target model's inherent behavior: they either disrupt the rollout using sub-optimal random intervention heuristics, or they enforce indiscriminate uniform supervision that unnecessarily overwrites the model's already-correct actions. We introduce JudgeMix, a judge-guided data synthesis framework that dynamically interleaves the target model and expert based on step-wise semantic evaluations. JudgeMix queries expert guidance precisely when the target model struggles, ensuring high trajectory success rates while keeping the state distribution aligned with the target model. It additionally uses the judge evaluation to reweight expert supervision on different steps, preserving model's inherent valid behavior while correcting its errors. On two agentic tool-use benchmarks, AppWorld and AutomationBench, JudgeMix demonstrates consistent superior performance to existing methods, with improvements up to 10 pass@1 points.

title: S1-Evo: Experience-Guided Evidence Competition Attacks on Typed System-1 Decision Models
summary: Typed System-1 (S1) decision models are increasingly deployed in LLM agents for routing, moderation, and authorization to cut inference cost, yet untrusted context can still manipulate typed outputs and alter execution branches. Unlike autoregressive System-2 (S2) models, S1 interfaces score dynamic rules and options without token-by-token decoding, mismatching attacks targeting text continuation or explicit override commands. We propose S1-Evo, a self-evolving framework tailored to S1's contract-based option competition and margin feedback. S1-Evo perturbs untrusted fields via contract-aware evidence channels to induce \emph{evidence competition} with original task evidence while preserving fact invariance. Offline on seed tasks, it optimizes candidates via feedback search guided by directional margins and re-verification, distilling verified flips into experience cards. At test time, S1-Evo retrieves relevant cards to construct perturbations for unseen tasks. Across four benchmarks and three S1 models, S1-Evo reaches 71.99\% mean ASR and 57.47\% high-confidence ASR on \texttt{jev-1.14}, and causes up to 24.00\% E2E agent violations.

title: AgentSSL: Can MLE Agents Leverage Unlabeled Data?
summary: Applying machine learning systems to new domains introduces bottlenecks in both labeled data acquisition and manual pipeline engineering. While recent MLE agents show promise in automating pipeline design, they have been studied almost exclusively in fully supervised settings, leaving them untested in realistic regimes where labeled data is scarce but unlabeled data is abundant. In this work, we introduce Agentic Semi-Supervised Learning (AgentSSL), framing SSL as a program search problem and studying how agents navigate this space under limited supervision. We find that even under weak feedback and matched compute, agents can synthesize code that combines and adapts established SSL techniques, exceeding the strongest human-engineered baselines in 8 of 12 settings by up to +21.8%. However, our results identify program selection as a critical bottleneck in AgentSSL, where performance drops by as much as 47% when selecting based on the agent's feedback metric. To systematically study this bottleneck, we introduce ProgramSelectBench, a large-scale benchmark with a combined total of 16,977 agent-generated and human-engineered SSL programs, and evaluate both unsupervised and active program selection methods. We further evaluate AgentSSL on real-world ecology detection tasks, highlighting the opportunities and challenges of transferring agent-discovered strategies beyond controlled benchmarks.

title: codex 0.169.0
summary:
New Features

  • The opt-in terminal workspace supports multiple side-chat tabs. Switch between them with the keyboard or mouse, and reopen saved local side chats after restarting Codex. (#59784, #60152, #60181)
  • Search older tasks from the agent command center by name, prompt preview, or working directory. (#60286)
  • Turn on Collapse turn details in the full-screen transcript to fold completed activity beneath each prompt while keeping answers visible and tool output searchable. (#60554, #60555, #60556, #60557)
  • Add or edit custom model providers from the terminal. With custom gateway onboarding enabled, you can create a provider during sign-in and use a device code for supported gateways over SSH or without a local browser. (#59779, #60009, #60186, #60486, #60662)
  • Press Ctrl+S in the terminal report editor to save a diagnostic ZIP locally, even when uploads are disabled. (#60542)
  • With the opt-in Cloud connection on macOS and Linux, send images, choose a model and reasoning effort, and archive or restore Cloud conversations from the terminal. (#59828, #60061, #60635, #60651)

Bug Fixes

  • codex exec keeps project configuration and MCP servers disabled in untrusted directories, even with --sandbox workspace-write. Use --trust with codex exec or codex review to explicitly save project trust. (#60041)
  • Yes, clear context and implement now hands the full approved plan to the fresh session and keeps the current session open if the handoff fails. (#60763)
  • Fixed Windows sandbox handling for quoted cmd.exe paths and for PowerShell sessions whose working directory has an unreadable parent. (#60624, #60647)
  • Pasted images on macOS retain their intended orientation and use native PNG or JPEG clipboard data when available. (#60455)
  • The terminal no longer stays busy waiting for MCP servers that a shared app server did not report. (#60280, #60622)
  • Interrupted turns now close cleanly, and delayed aborts or file approval cancellations no longer interrupt a later turn. (#59910, #60700)

Documentation

  • Updated the openai-docs skill to focus on Codex and ChatGPT Work questions and first-time API setup, with dedicated guidance for configuring Codex across a team. (#59944, #59949)
  • Documented how app-server clients can list models or authorize a gateway for a configured provider without changing the default provider. (#59776, #59819)

Chores

  • Updated bundled SQLite to 3.54 to pick up write-ahead log fixes. (#60432)
  • Plugin marketplace upgrades can reuse Git objects already on disk, reducing repeat downloads. (#60528)

title: We Are What We Remember: Mental-State-Driven Memory for Long-Term Character Dialogue
summary: Shared history in human dialogue is not merely a repository of facts, but the foundation of evolving relationships and mutual understanding. However, mainstream conversational memory systems rely on passive semantic similarity over external fact stores, frequently retrieving topically similar records while missing relationally pivotal experiences. Inspired by cognitive psychology's Self-Memory System (SMS), we propose MindMem, a mental-state-driven memory framework that asynchronously consolidates shared experiences into source-linked mental states of the character, the user, and their relationship. At each turn, a specialized mental-state reasoner (Mind) contextualizes these persistent states to anticipate latent user needs, form proactive intentions, and recover supporting episodic evidence that surface-level matching overlooks. To evaluate history-sensitive adaptation beyond factual recall, we introduce MemReal-Bench, a longitudinal benchmark grounded in month-long real-user interactions across dyadic and group scenes. By pairing Direct Question Answering (DQA) with Situated Memory Realization (SMR), it tests whether agents bridge the gap between knowing past facts and naturally using shared history, world rules, and relational trajectories. On MemReal-Bench, MindMem reaches 59.03% SMR and 82.58% DQA, exceeding the strongest memory baseline by 24.19 and 9.19 percentage points, respectively, and outperforming oracle target-memory injection on SMR. Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/jiazhicheng7-ctrl/MindMem.

title: Auditing AI peer reviewers: a benchmark on real scientific papers
summary: LLM-based peer review is now used at production scale, but its evaluation remains limited. We introduce a benchmark that injects objective, localisable errors of four types (general issues, mathematics, numerics, citations) at three severity levels into real papers and measures each reviewer's detection rate by error type and severity, together with its false-positive rate on clean copies. We also present Skepthical, a multi-agent reviewer that verifies citation-backed claims by retrieving the cited papers, mathematics with computer algebra, and numerical claims with executed code. We apply the benchmark to two corpora of 15 recent arXiv preprints each, one in astrophysics and one in machine learning (ML), injecting a total of 357 errors, and evaluate twelve reviewer systems: six single-LLM reviewers, two Claude Code configurations, three publicly available reviewers, and Skepthical. The choice of model has the largest impact on detection rate: given the same prompt, three frontier LLMs differ by about 50 percentage points in total detection on both corpora. Tools and scaffolding help when they contribute what the model cannot supply on its own. In particular, on astrophysics, Claude Code improves on a single Claude call in mathematics and numerics detection, and enforced citation retrieval gives Skepthical the highest citation error detection rate of all systems by a large margin. This citation lead, however, is not observed on ML, where the models appear to know the literature better and Skepthical's citation detection rate is statistically indistinguishable from that of the best single LLM. False-positive rates are below 10% for most systems, but vary with prompt, model, and scaffolding, with mathematics flags the main source of false positives. The evaluation pipeline, the injected errors, and the adjudication logs are released as a benchmark.

  • Fixed a message dropping out of a cloud session's conversation when the session restarted before Claude replied

  • Changed the claude mcp add --help example to a local command
  • Changed mods: a *, namespace or negated hook on engine.create now only observes. To add or withhold a $ noun, hook engine.create by name

  • Changed project (.mcp.json) MCP server approvals to match the server's exact name; an approval entry written in another spelling now asks again

  • Changed a /skill or @file typed between two files picked in claude.ai or the desktop app, or after a picked file and a link, to no longer take effect
  • Changed split-pane agent teammates to check that requests come from their team lead: one that outlives its lead has its asks refused, and plan approvals must be re-sent after /clear or /resume
  • Changed worktree creation to refuse checkouts whose .git folders are links or hold hard links, such as git-new-workdir layouts and cp -al copies; use a plain clone
  • Changed what Claude is told after safeguards stop a forked skill or a workflow agent: retry with a narrower prompt or tell you, instead of doing the work itself
  • Changed browser tool calls (Claude in Chrome, the desktop browser pane) to refuse some escaped or JSON-text inputs and tell Claude how to respell them
  • Changed workflows so that a prompt an app marks as not typed no longer reaches their agents as your request
  • Changed computer use on macOS to refuse key chords that hold Space with Control or Option, and more system shortcuts that need your grant
  • Changed first-run setup in Terminal.app to name the "Use Option as Meta key" setting, what Option stops typing, and how to undo it before you agree
  • Changed the maximum of CLAUDE_CODE_OVERLOADED_RETRY_MAX_DELAY_MS from 64000 to 300000
  • Changed workflows in the desktop app's Code tab to pause at a usage limit and continue after it resets
  • Changed the spend limit and 1M context errors, and /usage-credits, in cloud sessions and under Remote Control: they no longer give a web address
  • Changed which MCP servers are reported by name in OpenTelemetry exports to follow the current connector directory
